before.label: Geography & environmental inquiry
before.date_label: Nineteenth-century roots; regional, cultural and ecological inquiry
before.description: Several traditions ask how human activity and physical environments shape landscapes. Vidal investigates regional individuality; Marsh examines human environmental modification; Sauer relates physical and cultural forms; Leopold joins ecological observation with ethical concern. Their later uses differ, including Annales geography and environmental historians’ landscape inquiry. Critical and feminist geography add questions about capital, mobility, gender and contested place histories; Hayden and the History Workshop journal show specific historical uses. Driver examines the practices and disagreements of imperial geographical inquiry. Sauer’s historical reconstruction, Cosgrove’s criticism of visual neutrality and Febvre’s geographical collaborations reveal further disagreements within landscape inquiry.

before.scope_note: Vidal’s human geography and Marsh’s environmental inquiry are different resources; neither defines all later environmental history. This is a selective set of resources for historians, not a complete history of geography. Sauer and Leopold supply distinct approaches; national framing, ecological care and landscape morphology are not a single programme. Harvey and Massey disagree within critical inquiry; neither stands for the whole discipline. Colonial frameworks are investigated as historically situated practices with internal conflicts. This expanded selection still does not represent global geography comprehensively.

strands.title: Human activity and regional individuality
strands.focus: Vidal asks how human activity gives a region unity, within an explicitly French national frame.
strands.works: Tableau de la géographie de la France (1903)

strands.title: Human modification of physical environments
strands.focus: Marsh brings historical human action into inquiry about forests, waters and land; later historians recognize this precursor.

strands.title: Physical and cultural landscape forms
strands.focus: Sauer examines associations of landscape forms and their histories, resisting a rigid physical determinism.

strands.title: Ecological observation and landscape reading
strands.focus: Leopold’s observation and teaching connect ecological processes with human conduct; Cronon recalls a specific teaching inheritance.
strands.works: A Sand County Almanac (1949); Cronon’s retrospective afterword

strands.title: Human ecology and medical geography
strands.focus: Sorre’s project supplies a named geographical resource for conceptual inquiry.

strands.title: Mobility and unequal power
strands.focus: Massey asks who moves, who controls movement and how gender and colonial histories differentiate experience.

strands.title: Place, tradition and historical change
strands.focus: Massey disputes the necessary association of place identity with fixed tradition; Harvey allows valuable local resistance while questioning its sufficiency.

strands.title: Geographical resources in public history
strands.focus: Hayden uses Harvey while citing Massey’s feminist criticism in a project joining urban landscapes and public memory.

strands.title: Imperial networks and contested observation
strands.focus: Driver examines conflicting standards, instruments and observer credibility; colonial support did not make all geographical knowledge uniform.
strands.works: Geography’s Empire (1992); Hints to Travellers article (issue 1998)

strands.title: Reconstructing changing cultural landscapes
strands.focus: Sauer proposes reconstructing past cultural landscapes and their succession. His organic analogy is a working method rather than a literal biological law; claims of neutral observation and culture cycles remain open to criticism.

strands.title: Landscape as a historically situated way of seeing
strands.focus: Cosgrove explicitly challenges the neutrality of the areal concept and links visual conventions with property and power. His criticism of static chorology is placed beside Sauer’s own reconstruction of change, preserving disagreement.

strands.title: Historical inquiry, geographical resources and criticism
strands.focus: Vidal supplies methodological resources to Febvre; Sion encourages the project and Bataillon contributes notes. Sauer praises its criticism of environmentalism but questions its representation of geographical thought.
strands.works: La Terre et l’évolution humaine (1922); Sauer (1925); Febvre’s retrospective Combats essay

strands.title: Collaborative place history
strands.focus: The 1995 spatial-history section includes Rita and Jackie Huggins with Jane M. Jacobs. Verified coauthorship and the public finding aid document collaboration; detailed article interpretation remains limited by access.

before.label: Environmental history
before.description: Explains historical relations among people and the nonhuman world through ecological exchange, agriculture, property, commodity flows, conservation and cultural ideas of nature. These approaches disagree about causal emphasis. Cases from New England, the Great Plains, Mexico, India, colonial islands and South Africa connect ecological processes with power without supplying one universal model. Bullard’s environmental-justice inquiry and Rita and Jackie Huggins’s situated life histories broaden comparison toward unequal burdens, displacement and authority over historical accounts.
before.representative_figures_and_works: Alfred Crosby; Donald Worster; Carolyn Merchant; William Cronon. ASEH founded 1977. Expanded contextual readings include Leopold’s precursor essays, Melville’s Mexican study, Gadgil and Guha’s Indian history, Grove’s colonial conservation and Carruthers’s South African park history.

representative_people.context: Argues that organisms accompanying Europeans helped transform environments and sustain settler expansion, particularly in temperate regions.
representative_people.works: Ecological Imperialism: The Biological Expansion of Europe, 900–1900 (1986)

representative_people.context: Connects the Dust Bowl with agricultural capitalism as well as environmental conditions; this is a contested explanation, not the field’s unanimous account.

representative_people.context: Brings feminist history of science into environmental inquiry; argues that mechanical conceptions of nature support new forms of control and capitalist development.

representative_people.context: Links colonial property and ecological change, city–hinterland commodity flows, and cultural ideas of wilderness. His later afterword criticizes schematic capitalism and uneven treatment of Indigenous and colonial sources in his first book.
representative_people.works: Changes in the Land (1983); Nature’s Metropolis (1991); “The Trouble with Wilderness” (1995)

before.scope_note: Ecological exchange, political economy, and feminist critiques of nature overlap; institutional society history does not document every intellectual route. Crosby’s temperate-settler argument differs from Melville’s Mexican case; Gadgil and Guha’s resource conflicts differ from Grove’s conservation networks and Carruthers’s park politics. Cronon’s cultural account of wilderness does not deny nonhuman nature. The selection remains incomplete, especially in environmental justice and Indigenous scholarship. A bounded second-pass addition now compares Bullard and the Huggins collaboration; primary-excerpt, publisher-description and metadata limits remain distinct, and neither selection represents every community.

strands.title: Organisms, conquest and ecological exchange
strands.focus: Compare Crosby’s temperate settler environments with Melville’s explicit adaptation to grazing animals, land and continuing Indigenous populations in Mexico.
strands.works: Ecological Imperialism (1986); A Plague of Sheep (1994)

strands.title: Agricultural capitalism and environmental crisis
strands.focus: Worster connects the Dust Bowl to agricultural capitalism. Compare that argument with competing explanations instead of treating it as settled consensus.

strands.title: Gender, science and the control of nature
strands.focus: Merchant’s feminist intervention joins history of science with environmental questions; her mechanical-order argument concerns ideas, power and material change.

strands.title: Colonial property and ecological change
strands.focus: Property concepts help Cronon explain changes in New England. Read with his later self-criticism about source asymmetry, spirituality and schematic capitalism.
strands.works: Changes in the Land (1983; retrospective afterword 2003)

strands.title: Cities, commodities and hinterlands
strands.focus: Follow lumber, grain and meat between rural production and urban processing and markets; follow capital back toward the countryside.
strands.works: Nature’s Metropolis: Chicago and the Great West (1991)

strands.title: Resource use and social conflict in India
strands.focus: Changing resource-use systems, state interventions and resistance connect ecological and social histories without making precolonial society uniformly harmonious.

strands.title: Conservation, colonial science and racial power
strands.focus: Grove studies colonial conservation networks and islands; Carruthers studies a South African park’s racial and national politics. These distinct scales complicate a purely benevolent conservation story.
strands.works: Green Imperialism (1995); The Kruger National Park (1995)

strands.title: Wilderness as a historical cultural idea
strands.focus: Cronon examines the pristine-wilderness ideal and Indigenous removal, while defending care for nonhuman nature in inhabited places.

strands.title: Historical geography in environmental-history teaching
strands.focus: Cronon’s 1994 syllabus assigns Sauer’s 1941 essay among several resources for bringing nature into history. Assignment demonstrates use without establishing assent or an exclusive intellectual ancestry.

strands.title: Unequal pollution burdens and collective action
strands.focus: Bullard joins environmental distribution with race, class and organizing capacity. The Alsen case distinguishes partial gains from unresolved health concerns and internal disagreement.
strands.works: Dumping in Dixie (1990), selected reprinted excerpts

strands.title: Country, displacement and historical voice
strands.focus: Read Rita and Jackie Huggins’s situated life-history project beside conservation and settler-landscape narratives. Publisher descriptions support this bounded comparison; their full books and place article remain unread.
strands.works: Auntie Rita (1994); Changes in the Land (1983); The Kruger National Park (1995)

strands.title: Organisms, conquest and ecological exchange
strands.focus: Compare Crosby’s temperate settler environments with Melville’s explicit adaptation to grazing animals, land and continuing Indigenous populations in Mexico.
strands.works: Ecological Imperialism (1986); A Plague of Sheep (1994)

strands.title: Agricultural capitalism and environmental crisis
strands.focus: Worster connects the Dust Bowl to agricultural capitalism. Compare that argument with competing explanations instead of treating it as settled consensus.

strands.title: Gender, science and the control of nature
strands.focus: Merchant’s feminist intervention joins history of science with environmental questions; her mechanical-order argument concerns ideas, power and material change.

strands.title: Colonial property and ecological change
strands.focus: Property concepts help Cronon explain changes in New England. Read with his later self-criticism about source asymmetry, spirituality and schematic capitalism.
strands.works: Changes in the Land (1983; retrospective afterword 2003)

strands.title: Cities, commodities and hinterlands
strands.focus: Follow lumber, grain and meat between rural production and urban processing and markets; follow capital back toward the countryside.
strands.works: Nature’s Metropolis: Chicago and the Great West (1991)

strands.title: Resource use and social conflict in India
strands.focus: Changing resource-use systems, state interventions and resistance connect ecological and social histories without making precolonial society uniformly harmonious.

strands.title: Conservation, colonial science and racial power
strands.focus: Grove studies colonial conservation networks and islands; Carruthers studies a South African park’s racial and national politics. These distinct scales complicate a purely benevolent conservation story.
strands.works: Green Imperialism (1995); The Kruger National Park (1995)

strands.title: Wilderness as a historical cultural idea
strands.focus: Cronon examines the pristine-wilderness ideal and Indigenous removal, while defending care for nonhuman nature in inhabited places.

strands.title: Historical geography in environmental-history teaching
strands.focus: Cronon’s 1994 syllabus assigns Sauer’s 1941 essay among several resources for bringing nature into history. Assignment demonstrates use without establishing assent or an exclusive intellectual ancestry.

strands.title: Unequal pollution burdens and collective action
strands.focus: Bullard joins environmental distribution with race, class and organizing capacity. The Alsen case distinguishes partial gains from unresolved health concerns and internal disagreement.
strands.works: Dumping in Dixie (1990), selected reprinted excerpts

strands.title: Country, displacement and historical voice
strands.focus: Read Rita and Jackie Huggins’s situated life-history project beside conservation and settler-landscape narratives. Publisher descriptions support this bounded comparison; their full books and place article remain unread.
strands.works: Auntie Rita (1994); Changes in the Land (1983); The Kruger National Park (1995)

strands.title: Agricultural culture, technology and regional causes
strands.focus: Worster argues for interacting natural and cultural forces while emphasizing agricultural capitalism. McDean criticizes his generalization, contests Bonnifield’s federal-policy account and favors Hurt’s regional specificity. These are competing interpretations.
strands.works: Worster (1986); McDean (1986), discussing books of 1979 and 1981

strands.title: Ecological adaptation and the promise of development
strands.focus: Worster acknowledges Malin’s ecological history but disputes explanations through natural storms and a passing pioneering stage. He distinguishes rival cultural values and varied regional entrepreneurial intensity.

strands.title: Regional boundaries and histories of staying
strands.focus: Compare McDean’s insistence on a specific Dust Bowl region, Fite’s call for northern Plains coverage, and Riney-Kehrberg’s household survival study in southwestern Kansas. Causal explanation, geographical scale and lived experience pose different questions.

before.relationship: Marsh, Leopold and Sauer supply distinct resources for environmental historical inquiry and teaching
before.evidence_note: Marsh is an environmental precursor; do not derive every environmental-history tradition from Vidal or Annales. Lowenthal documents Marsh’s environmental-history relevance; Cronon recalls workshops modeled on Leopold’s course. These are distinct historical resources, not one direct genealogy. A further named teaching use is Cronon’s Fall 1994 History 901 assignment of Sauer’s 1941 Foreword to Historical Geography. This is separate from the 1925 Morphology essay and establishes a syllabus use, not universal reception.

Worster explicitly rejects monocausal ecological history (108), critically receives Malin, distinguishes entrepreneurial values from rival farming cultures (113), and allows varying intensity across regions (note17). His interpretation of 1977 imagery and predictions about later dust storms are historical arguments, not independently audited scientific findings. outcomes.finding: McDean’s complete available article and Worster’s complete 1986 argument now distinguish Bonnifield’s federal-policy criticism, Hurt’s regional agricultural explanation and Malin’s adaptation account. Worster’s explicit rejection of monocausal history and acknowledgment of rival farming cultures qualify abbreviated summaries. Fite’s call for northern coverage contrasts with McDean’s bounded region; Riney-Kehrberg adds the social history of staying. Hewes is a specifically cited geographical resource.
outcomes.research_limit: Complete available McDean and Worster OCR traversed including notes, with interleaved columns and some missing tokens; original PDFs unavailable and no scan collation. McDean PDF local/escalated 403, CORE404. Fite displayed repository text read, original PDF not collated. Riney-Kehrberg publisher description/contents, not book body; original publication/format chronology separated. Malin, Bonnifield, Hurt and Hewes originals remain unread; interpretations are attributed to named reviewers. No empirical validation of historical climatology, interviews or agricultural datasets. McDean’s claim of settled causes and bias-free Hurt is not adopted.
